entries.title: House Republican Men Are Behaving Badly, Endangering Their Seats And The Majority
entries.summary: Facing ethics allegations, those lawmakers who refuse to end their campaigns could face the wrath of voters in November.
entries.content:
Chuck Edwards was supposed to be the safe choice.

“He is the embodiment of mountain values who will fight for them every single day in Congress with honor and integrity,” Sen. Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina) said in May 2022, after Edwards ousted a controversial one-term incumbent.

Four years later the North Carolina Republican faced a bipartisan rebuke from the House Ethics Committee, which recommended a rare censure motion for inappropriate behavior with young female staff.

“It’s going to be problematic for his campaign,” Tillis told reporters Monday evening.

A little after 3 a.m. Wednesday, Edwards dropped out of his reelection bid, leaving state Republican officials scramblingto find a replacement candidate.

Edwards is one of several Republican men in the House who face allegations that have put what should be reasonably safe districts in political jeopardy.

Reps. Max Miller (R-Ohio) and Cory Mills (R-Florida) are also under investigation by the Ethics Committee for, among other allegations, assaulting a woman (Mills) and domestic violence (Miller). Tony Gonzales, a three-term Republican from South Texas, resigned earlier this year after admitting to an affair with a staffer who later committed suicide. He was headed to likely defeat in a primary runoff to Brandon Herrera, who is now facing questions about demeaning comments he has posted about women.

In each instance, the lawmakers denied the allegations and, at least initially, asserted they would remain in their reelection campaigns. Republicans, already on the defensive amid President Donald Trump’s deep unpopularity, must now devote resources to defending red seats that shouldn’t be on the radar as competitive.

In 2024, Trump won all four of these districts by wide margins, ranging from almost 10 percentage points to 15 points. In the last 2024 analysis by The Cook Political Report With Amy Walter, none of these seats appeared on the chart of the roughly 70 most competitive House races in the country.

Now, all four are ranked among the three dozen toughest races for Republicans to defend in November.

Walter, the Cook report’s editor-in-chief, compared the current environment to the 2006 midterms,when Republicans lost 30 seats and the majority as President George W. Bush was mired in the Iraq war with terrible approval ratings.

“This year feels like déjà vu. … In both years: Unpopular war, Members mired in sex scandals,” she wrote.

In past midterm elections, however, these ethics-infused defeats did not tip the balance of power in the House, as the waves were so high that the majority party was largely doomed. But through mid-decade redistricting and a huge financial edge, today’s House Republicans have the type of political flood insurance their predecessors lacked.

They might be able to use these advantages to hold the majority by the narrowest of margins — unless several of these scandal-plagued seats fall to Democrats.

In 2006, Democrats padded their new majority by claiming a handful of seats in which Republican incumbents faced unique allegations.

Don Sherwood (R-Pennsylvania), who had won his previous two races with more than 80 percent of the vote, lost his race amid allegations that he had assaulted a mistress. John Sweeney (R-New York), a onetime rising star who had won his previous three races with more than 65 percent, lost after a report about a 911 call from his wife alleging an assault.

Mark Foley (R-Florida), who had won his previous two races by more than 35 percentage points each, resigned just weeks before the 2006 election amid an ethics investigation into sexually explicit conversations with teenage House pages, handing the seat to Democrats.

A few safe Republicans faced their own corruption investigations, including Tom DeLay (R-Texas), the House majority leader, and Bob Ney (R-Ohio), chair of the House Administration Committee. Both resigned midterm, and Republicans couldn’t hold on to those seats.

In 2010, Democrats lost their majority in a historic 63-seat loss that mostly centered around high unemployment and a conservative revolt against big government spending. But Bob Etheridge (D-North Carolina), who had won four straight races with more than 65 percent of the vote, stumbled, almost literally, into political trouble. A few young Republican operatives caught him leaving an evening fundraiser and, on video, asked about his policy positions.

Etheridge lunged toward them, grabbing one of them and repeatedly asked, “Who are you, who are you?” A neophyte opponent latched onto the viral video and gained attention, narrowly defeating him by 1 percentage point that fall.

In 2018, the political wave that swept Democrats back into power was foretold by Tim Murphy (R-Pennsylvania), who was so popular as a conservative anti-abortion Republican that Democrats did not field an opponent in his last two re-elections. But Murphy resigned in late 2017 after admitting to an affairwith a woman who accused him of pressuring her to get an abortion.

In early 2018, despite the district’s deep conservative lean, Conor Lamb, the Democratic candidate, won the special election to replace Murphy and established a playbook for other Democrats in tough districts for distancing themselves from the national party brand — ending with a more than 40-seat gain that November for Democrats.

In each of these cases, it’s a relatively safe bet that had the incumbent remained free of ethical challenges — or had they given their party more time to find an appropriate replacement — the party in power would have won those races.

That’s why Republicans this year pushed Gonzales to resign — and why some have tried to push Edwards and Miller to remove themselves from the November ballot.

And in Florida, Republican Reps. Mike Haridopolos and Anna Paulina Luna took the rare move to oppose an incumbent in their delegation, siding against Millsahead of the primary later this month.

“We need leaders in Congress who serve with integrity, energy, and an unwavering commitment to the people who sent them there,” the two Republicans wrote.

In addition to “other allegations,” the Ethics Committee is also reviewing the circumstances involving a second woman who got a restraining order against Mills last fall. But Trump has endorsed Mills, whose opposition could split among several Republican challengers.

Democrats believe Bale Dalton, a Navy veteran and former NASA official, provides the right contrast in November if Mills wins the nomination later this month.

Democrats are particularly bullish on defeating Miller, whose ex-father-in-law, Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio), said that Miller posed such a danger that he moved his wife, daughter and granddaughter out of state to protect them.

“The allegations here are horrible, and it’s really disqualifying behavior,” Rep. Suzan DelBene (D-Washington), chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, told Scott MacFarlane Reports, an independent news organization covering Congress.

Miller, who won his last election by 15 points, has defended himself in a series of media appearances that only further raised alarms. Ohio law could allow Republicans to replace Miller by Monday, but that only can occur if Miller willingly steps aside, a scenario he is publicly rejecting.

“No one has told me to get off the ballot, and that’s because they know I can win,” Miller told CNN’s Jake Tapper on Monday.

Sometimes the replacement candidates come with their own political baggage, as is the case in Texas. Herrera’s recent career as an edgy YouTuber, filled with comments some consider misogyny, does not create the type of distance from Gonzales’ actions that most Republicans would prefer.

On Thursday, the DCCC added the district to its “Red to Blue” list as a designated battleground, a move that Republicans believe ignores the strong conservative lean of the district.

“All they will buy is another expensive humiliation in November,” Christian Martinez, an official with the National Republican Congressional Committee, told The Texas Tribune.

Past speakers tried to deal swiftly with transgressions to limit the exposure other caucus members faced in having to defend rogue colleagues. Foley and Murphy were pushed out in a matter of weeks. Speaker Mike Johnson, however, has been more reluctant to use his moral megaphone to push members aside, in part because his single-digit majority needs every possible vote to succeed.

In Edwards case, four years ago he was the replacement candidate himself.

Madison Cawthorn (R-North Carolina) had a high-profile single term in the House, fueled by uncorroborated stories about his escape from a car crash and his bid to attend the U.S. Naval Academy. Cawthorn alleged that many members of Congress attended parties with drugs and prostitutes, a story that lit up online and forced lawmakers to defend themselves against back home.

Led by Tillis, senior North Carolina Republicans rallied around Edwards, who made millions as a McDonald’s franchisee before serving six years in the state Senate. He was sold as the pure candidate, no controversy, narrowly defeating the young far-right ideologue in the May 2022 primary.

In its report released Monday, the Ethics Committee found that over several years Edwards showered two younger female aides with gifts, hand-written letters and other mementos that were sexual in nature.

“We seem to have a fondness for many of the same things,” he wrote to one aide. “Even where we do not, I’ll enjoy the adventure alongside you!"

His adventure ended Wednesday with his withdrawal from the election, and now North Carolina’s Republican leaders are searching for a new candidate. But Edwards will complete his current term, a sign of how much Johnson still needs his vote.

entries.title: A Capital Bikeshare Ride to Remember
entries.content:
Good morning, D.C. In today’s newsletter: a Capital Bikeshare pioneer, a very loud IndyCar race and a birthday boy at the National Zoo. 





THE LATEST

Capital Bikeshare challenge, accepted.

Earlier this summer, D.C. resident Andy Jarrin decided that his short jaunts on Capital Bikeshare — the region’s red rentable bikes — weren’t enough.

“I had seen people post their longest rides ever on [New York’s] Citi Bikes and Capital Bikeshare, and the rides didn’t seem that long,” he tells NOTUS. “I wondered, what is the longest distance someone could go between two stations.”

The answer took him 42 miles from a station in Largo, Maryland, to another just beyond Reston, Virginia. It took Jarrin, an energetic 26-year-old, just over four hours to finish the ride — and he didn’t stop along the way.

From what NOTUS can gather — and Capital Bikeshare tentatively confirmed — Jarrin’s ride may stand as the single longest continuous ride on a non-electric Bikeshare bike. We’re told someone rode 54.9 miles on an electric Bikeshare, a feat worthy of its own respect.

Mind you: The recognizable red bikes aren’t Tour de France-worthy steeds, though years ago another brave soul did use one to complete a triathlon. Each bike weighs some 40 pounds and has limited gears. Jarrin admits the worst part of the adventure was climbing westward from Georgetown into Arlington County on the Custis Trail.

The Capital Bikeshare network started in 2010 and has since expanded to include more than 8,000 bikes and 800 docking stations across the D.C. region. There have been more than 2.8 million rides on the bikes through June of this year. Jarrin discovered the bike network when he moved to D.C. from Miami three years ago.

“It was something new,” he says. “Everything is so car-centric back in Miami, so having so many bike lanes and bikes was a good change of pace.”

Are there any other Bikeshare challenges to come? Jarrin won’t say no, but he also thinks he’s now fully justified in graduating to the world of bike ownership. “Right now I want to get on a better bike and do long rides,” he says.





FROM THE DISTRICT

Jeanine Pirro took on the role of D.C.’s top prosecutor with two personas: a bombastic Fox News host willing to pursue politically charged issues with zeal, and a former Westchester County prosecutor and judge who wants to run a U.S. attorney’s office with a sense of normalcy. President Donald Trump’s botched Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool project put those sides at odds — and her job at risk, report NOTUS’ Jose Pagliery and Derek Hawkins.

Too fast, too furious, too f’ing loud. The National Gallery of Art studied how vibrations from the upcoming Freedom 250 Grand Prix would affect art, The Washington Post reports. The museum declined to share its specific findings, but some preservationists are concerned about the risk.

A group dubbed the “D.C. rat rangers” is walking the city’s wards by night to teach residents how to keep rodents at bay, Axios D.C. reports.

Howard University is offering buyouts to 600 employees as the school continues to face financial strain, The Chronicle of Higher Education reports. The voluntary buyouts were first offered in June to full-time faculty members or staff with at least 10 years of continuous employment — criteria that covers nearly 16% of the university’s workforce. They have until this fall to apply to the buyout program.





FROM VIRGINIA

Gov. Abigail Spanberger announced in a Washington Post op-ed that she’ll be “intervening” in the proposed $67 billion energy merger between NextEra and Dominion. That means she’ll formally request to be a party when regulators weigh the deal, which would create the world’s largest regulated electric utility.





FROM MARYLAND

A new state commission will study the deaths of at least 230 Black boys buried between 1870 and 1939 outside a juvenile facility with a documented history of abuse, The Washington Post reports.





METRO MOMENTS

Bao Li AP - 26217046150810 (7360x4912, AR: 1.50)
Happy birthday to the National Zoo’s Bao Li, who turned 5 this week. Giant pandas — they grow up so fast.

Have an image from around D.C. you want to share? A question for our reporters? An “only in D.C.” moment? Tell us about it.



SPORTS

It’s been a good summer for the Washington Spirit. On Thursday, coach Adrián González was named NWSL coach of the month for July, while forward Trinity Rodman earned player of the month honors. The 24-year-old Rodman collected five goals and an assist on the month, helping her team to a 5-1 record.

Just more than halfway through the regular season, Washington has the second-best record in the league, trailing Gotham by one point. The Spirit hosts the North Carolina Courage on Saturday night.

What to Watch Today

MLB: Nationals vs. Reds, 6:45 p.m. (Fox 5)

WNBA: Mystics vs. Dream, 7:30 p.m. (ION)

entries.title: ‘No Idea What We’re Going to Do’
entries.content:
Today’s notice: Senate still stuck. Voters oust Ogles. Republicans practice El-Sayed’s full name. Next stop in the progressive vs. establishment battle: Hawaii. And: midterm déjà vu.





THE LATEST

We’re going to overtime: The Senate was supposed to leave town today for a long recess. But that’s not happening — there’s still a lot to be done and little time left to do it. And so a group incredibly eager to get some distance from Washington as soon as possible is forced to stick around and possibly work the weekend and into next week.

Will that be enough time? We’re still waiting to find out. The agenda remains pretty stacked with unknown outcomes — will Todd Blanche get the votes he needs to be confirmed as attorney general? He’s still short, per the official count. There’s also a fight about hemp regulations that needs to be resolved before a stopgap spending bill can be passed.

And, the Russia sanctions bill, which saw quick movement after the death of Sen. Lindsey Graham, is still awaiting action.

Or, as summed up by Sen. John Kennedy (R-Louisiana): “I still have no idea what we’re going to do, and if we do something, when we’re going to do it.”

So it’s a lot of nail-biter Senate dealmaking action. But the real drama starts when these lawmakers get back home to voters who want answers on the agenda items they didn’t get to — the Iran war, the SAVE America Act and on and on.

Open tabs: McConnell Says He’s Been Released From Rehabilitation Facility to Recover at Home (NOTUS); Women’s Share of Top Military Promotions Plunged This Year (NYT); White House Begins Head Start Program Overhaul (NOTUS); The new fight over who gets to be ‘working class’ (Politico); Author of DNC’s 2024 “autopsy” says he concluded Gaza war hurt Harris (Axios)





From the campaign trail


Andy Ogles sent home: Republican primary voters in Tennessee’s redrawn 5th Congressional District voted out the controversial member of Congress last night. Former state Agriculture Commissioner Charlie Hatcher won the Republican nomination in what was drawn to be a safe seat for the GOP.

A few takeaways: First, it’s another defeat for a Trump-backed candidate. The president hosted a tele-rally for Ogles just last week. Hatcher had the endorsement of Gov. Bill Lee. Second: This can be seen as a victory for the clean energy industry, which targeted Ogles with negative ads. Third: Ogles was routinely in the news for the wrong reasons, most notoriously drawing criticism from his fellow Republicans for a post that said, “Homosexuality has no place in America.” (He blamed a staffer.) But he was also rebuked by some Senate Republicans for Islamophobic rhetoric, which is a bit ironic given this next item coming up.

El-Sayed on his newly popular full name: “This is the best place in the world to be Abdul,” the freshly minted Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan — home to one of America’s largest Arab populations — told reporters this week. Republicans seem to think his name is a liability, NOTUS’ Angie Orellana Hernandez reports. Immediately after he was declared the primary winner, the NRSC sent out a press release referring to him as Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, rather than the name he’s used for his entire political career. It was a formulation the committee had not used previously.

Eyes on Hawaii: Another progressive vs. establishment battle is set for Saturday between state Democratic Sen. Jarrett Keohokalole and longtime Rep. Ed Case. Case, who has served seven nonconsecutive terms in Congress, is touting his seniority and ability as an appropriator to bring federal dollars home, NOTUS’ Christa Dutton tells us. Keohokalole’s pitch is that it’s time for change, especially after Case voted with Republicans on an early version of the SAVE Act and didn’t sign a letter with his fellow Hawaii Democrats condemning ICE raids.

Momentum is on Keohokalole’s side after progressive wins against incumbents in New York City and Denver, but Hawaii is an old-school Democratic state that isn’t quick to welcome change, said Colin Moore, a political scientist at the University of Hawaii at Mānoa. “Because progressive challenges to the Democratic establishment traditionally haven’t done all that well here, I think it would show that this anti-incumbency sense among the Democratic electorate is much broader than just very progressive Western or Northeastern areas,” Moore said.

From the White House


Another bite at birthright: With two new executive orders yesterday, the president made it clear he plans to continue trying to limit the constitutional rules around birthright citizenship, despite the Supreme Court decision earlier this year batting down his first attempt. NOTUS’ Manuela Silva details the new orders, one of which claims powers to deny citizenship to some children born in the U.S. under certain circumstances, while the other directs federal officials to deny visas to travelers coming to the U.S. for “birth tourism.”

From the courts


A federal judge ordered the Trump administration to pay several nonprofits by today at noon Pacific Time for the legal services they provided to unaccompanied migrant children, NOTUS’ Jackie Llanos reports. The Office of Refugee Resettlement, tasked with the care of the children, had withheld millions in reimbursements for legal representation since December because the nonprofits declined to provide information about their minor clients to protect their privacy. The office just gave a new sole-source, $150 million contract to a small Texas firm.





NEW ON NOTUS

House Republican scandals lead to midterm déjà vu: In a previous midterm where historical trends were on their side, 2006, Democrats were able to make their blue wave splash a little further up the beach thanks to a slew of scandals by Republican lawmakers that made them vulnerable in otherwise safe seats. Our Paul Kane looks back at that cycle and compares it to this one in his latest for NOTUS. That déjà vu line came from the Cook Political Report’s Amy Walter, who said, “In both years: unpopular war, members mired in sex scandals.”

More: Rep. Julie Johnson Violated Transparency Law With Dozens of Late Stock Disclosures, by Dave Levinthal

DOJ Sued Over Trump Tax-Audit Immunity Deal, by Jenna Monnin

Some Visa Applicants Could Pay Up to $250K in Bonds to Overcome Denials, by Jenna Monnin





NOT US

  • Moderate Democrats Prepare for ‘War’ Against an Ascendant Left, by Shane Goldmacher for The New York Times
  • Bobby Pulido is sick and tired of apologizing, by Samuel Benson for Politico
  • Senate Republicans launch network of fake news sites, by Judd Legum for Popular Information

entries.title: Retiring Sen. Gary Peters Is Already Negotiating His Next Gig
entries.summary: The Michigan senator’s term ends early next year.
entries.content:
Sen. Gary Peters is slated to represent Michigan on Capitol Hill for another five months. He’s already eyeing new opportunities on the West Coast.

A Senate ethics document reviewed by NOTUS indicates that Peters, a two-term Senate Democrat who isn’t seeking reelection this year, is negotiating employment with the University of Southern California.

The negotiations began on June 3, according to the ethics document, which Peters signed the same day.

Peters’ office confirmed that the senator “is having conversations about potential opportunities once he completes his Senate term.”

“He is following all Senate rules regarding future employment opportunities,” the office told NOTUS in a statement. “There are no additional details to share at this time.”

Senate ethics rules in part mandate that senators “must avoid not only an actual conflict of interest, but also the appearance of a conflict between their duties to the Senate and the interests of the prospective employers with whom they are negotiating.”

Representatives for the University of Southern California did not respond to phone and email messages requesting comment.

It’s unclear what kind of job Peters is seeking with the university or where he’d be located.

In addition to its main campus in Los Angeles, the University of South California has a “Capital Campus” in Washington, D.C., with a mission to “accelerate our influence and impact, promote and develop strong leaders, and forge critical partnerships to address the nation’s most pressing issues and opportunities.

It also has a sizable government relations operation, which typically spends hundreds of thousands of dollars each year on federal-level lobbying efforts.

This year alone, the University of Southern California has lobbied several government agencies, Congress and the White House on a variety of topics, ranging from higher education policy to national security and defense research, according to federal records.

entries.title: Cassidy Says He Will Back Blanche, Paving Way for Confirmation
entries.summary: The Louisiana Republican was the deciding vote on President Trump's nominee to lead the Justice Department.
entries.content:
Louisiana Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy announced that he will support acting Attorney General Todd Blanche’s nomination to lead the Justice Department, handing him enough votes to confirm him as early as later today before the Senate leaves for the August break.

“All considered, I will vote for Mr. Blanche,” Cassidy said in a speech on the Senate floor.

Cassidy defended Blanche on a number of fronts. He noted that Blanche was not the decider of pardons given out to Jan. 6 rioters and that even when he gives advice, President Donald Trump does not have to listen.

He also dismissed the acrimonious history between him and Trump, who endorsed his opponent earlier this year in his Senate primary race after Cassidy voted to convict him of his actions after Jan. 6, 2021.

“This is not a referendum on President Trump. It is the decision regarding Mr. Blanche in very specific circumstances,” Cassidy said. “I’ll be criticized for this decision, what’s new? The people of Louisiana can be assured that I worked hard to understand the issue and to make the right decision.”

Cassidy noted that he and Blanche spoke numerous times throughout the confirmation process, having just got off the phone with him right before his speech.

The move comes hours after Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) announced her opposition to Blanche’s nomination.

Much like Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) earlier in the week, Murkowski faulted Blanche for green-lighting the settlement with President Donald Trump that spawned the $1.8 billion Justice Department fund and the immunity deal that would have shielded Trump from future IRS audits.

Both parts of the deal have drawn widespread derision among Senate Republicans. That prompted Sens. John Cornyn (R-Texas) and Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina) to push for an in-writing agreement that nixes the “slush” fund, which would have provided settlements to the Trump allies and Jan. 6, 2021 rioters, and the scope of the immunity accord.

Murkowski cast doubt that the issue will go away after a potential confirmation.

“I am also keenly aware that the Department’s nearly $2-billion dollar slush fund—which likely would have rewarded January 6 protesters—is only off the table because this nomination is pending and the Senate has leverage,” Murkowski said. “Once we vote, that will end, and there is no telling what the future holds.”

“The country needs an Attorney General who will check the worst impulses of this administration,” she continued. “I hope Mr. Blanche is able to achieve that, if confirmed, but I simply do not have confidence that will be the case.”

Murkowski also cited Blanche's handling of the files related to crimes committed by Jeffrey Epstein, statements he reportedly made to pro-life groups and the DOJ’s attempt to indict Sens. Mark Kelly (D-Arizona) and Elissa Slotkin (D-Michigan) over videos encouraging military members to resist unlawful orders.
